the settling velocity of TSS from WWFs is higher than that of particulate pollutants and that it is also higher than that from dry weather sewage or pavement runoff.
the settleability of particulate pollutants is significantly lower than that of TSS and is also lower than that of pollutants from urban pavement runoff.

the settling velocity of TSS and particulate pollutants (heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, phosphorus) from combined sewer wet-weather discharges (WWF).
the settling behaviour of particulates from combined sewer WWF, which is of importance to the design of settling facilities.

the following aspects: 1) the settling behaviour of the particulate pollutants in the combined sewer system is different from the behaviour of the total suspended solids (TSS); 2) the settleability of the micropollutants varies significantly depending on the parameter considered; 3) a decrease in settleability of TSS is observed between small and large scaled catchments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the settling behaviour of particulates in WWF is not a constant and that the settling velocity of particulate micropollutants cannot be deduced from the settling velocity of TSS.
the settleability of particulate pollutants depends not only on the considered pollutant, but also on its distribution over the particle size spectrum.
, depending on the pollutant and the considered catchment, settling velocities may be either lower or higher than the reference values used in France.

the design of settling tanks should be based on TSS measurements, but that the removal of micropollutants should be considered separately.

the settleability of micropollutants in WWFs is not a simple function of the settleability of TSS, and the design of settling tanks for micropollutant removal should not rely on the settleability of the TSS.

the settling velocity of particulate micropollutants in WWFs is not necessarily lower than in dry weather sewers and can even be significantly higher.
